one_liner: Python reference code for fast PLBF and PLBF++, which cut partitioned learned Bloom filter construction time 34x-761x versus PLBF.
what_it_does: A partitioned learned Bloom filter (PLBF) takes a classifier score s(x) in [0,1] for each key and splits the score range into N equal segments. Dynamic programming groups those segments into k regions, and each region gets a backup Bloom filter with its own FPR. This repo implements PLBF, fast PLBF and fast PLBF++ as Python classes in two versions: minimize memory for a target FPR F (PLBF, FastPLBF, FastPLBFpp), or minimize expected FPR under a memory budget M (the *_M classes, which the paper's experiments use). The constructor takes (pos_keys, pos_scores, neg_scores, F or M, N, k) and queries are contains(key, score). You bring your own model and its scores, and the CLI scripts read a CSV of key,label,score.
how_it_is_fast: PLBF solves a separate O(j^2 k) DP for each j = k..N, which is O(N^3 k) in total. Fast PLBF observes that every one of those subproblems is a prefix of the single j = N table, so it builds that table once and traces back each j in O(k). That gives O(N^2 k) with an identical result. Fast PLBF++ also treats each DP layer as a row-maxima 'matrix problem' on a monotone matrix (Aggarwal et al. 1987) and solves it by divide-and-conquer: exhaustively search the middle row, then recurse on the narrowed ranges (matrix_problem_on_monotone_matrix.py). That gives O(Nk log N + Nk^2). Monotonicity is proven only for an 'ideal' score distribution where g_i/h_i is non-decreasing; otherwise the result can be suboptimal.
when_to_use: You use or plan to use a PLBF, and the parameter search dominates build time at N around 1000. The paper reports PLBF spending over 3 minutes finding t and f, while fast PLBF and fast PLBF++ finish the whole build in under 2 seconds.
The filter is rebuilt often (model retraining, changing key sets), so construction latency matters more than query speed.
You want to raise N and k to lower FPR without cubic build cost. The authors suggest N ~1000 and k ~100, with builds of a few tens of seconds.
Pick fast PLBF when you need exactly PLBF's thresholds and FPRs. Pick fast PLBF++ when classifier scores are close to monotone and an FPR penalty of about 0.2% (URLs) is acceptable.
You want a compact reference for porting the DP into your own C++ or Rust learned filter. The core is about 100 lines across calc_DPKL.py, fast_calc_DPKL.py and matrix_problem_on_monotone_matrix.py.
when_not_to_use: On a production query path. Backup filters use the pure-Python bloom-filter 1.3.3 package, contains() does a Python bisect plus Python hashing, and the paper reports no query-throughput numbers. The speedup is build-time only.

When you have no classifier that produces [0,1] scores at query time. Every lookup needs s(x), so model inference cost and model size (312 Kb and 1.19 Mb LightGBM models in the paper) add to each query and to total memory.

When scores are weakly correlated with membership, use fast PLBF++ with care. It is not guaranteed optimal, and on synthetic data with almost no monotonicity (10^8 swaps) its FPR reached 1.85x PLBF's (paper Appendix G). Use fast PLBF there.

When the baseline you actually run is the original public PLBF code (kapilvaidya24/plbf). That code appears to run one DP over at most 100 quantile chunks, which is the 'relaxed' method. Appendix F shows the relaxed method builds about as fast as fast PLBF, although its FPR is up to 1.48x worse on EMBER. The 34x-761x figures are against the O(N^3 k) complete method.
When you need dynamic inserts or deletes. Keys go in once at construction, into fixed-size backup Bloom filters, and there is no update or serialization API.

integration.form: source-drop. There is no setup.py or pyproject and it is not on PyPI; the scripts prepend the parent directory to sys.path. The MIT code is also vendored in the pip package learnedbf (SLIMlaboratory, Apache-2.0).
integration.dependencies: bloom-filter==1.3.3 (pure Python), pandas==2.3.0, scikit-learn==1.6.1. PLBF.py imports pandas and scikit-learn at module top level even though only the CLI uses them.
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.9+ (inferred: signatures use list[float] annotations, and the pinned pandas 2.3.0 and scikit-learn 1.6.1 require >=3.9); not otherwise documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — FastPLBF and FastPLBFpp subclass the repo's own PLBF class, keep the same constructor and contains(key, score), and override only find_best_t_and_f. They are not API-compatible with the original kapilvaidya24/plbf functions (get_thresholds, get_optimal_fpr).

gotchas: Inputs are validated with assert statements, one per score. Running under python -O strips them, and when they are active they add an O(n) Python loop to construction.

A June 2025 commit ('fix counting method') switched to add-one smoothing: segment and region counts now start at 1 and totals include the pseudo-counts. The current code is therefore not identical to the code behind the 2023 paper numbers.

In PLBF_M and FastPLBF_M, memory_usage_of_backup_bf is computed from the last loop iteration's t and f, not from t_best and f_best, so the reported figure may not match the configuration chosen. The filters themselves are built with the best values.
Segments are equal-width score intervals (i/N), not quantiles as in the original plbf code, so heavily skewed score distributions leave many segments nearly empty.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet. Compared with the baseline PLBF code, pick this when you need the complete, fi <= 1-constrained optimum at large N or k in seconds. If you want a pip-installable wrapper with scikit-learn-style classifiers, learnedbf vendors this code.
verified_claims_summary: The NeurIPS 2023 paper times Python construction (including LightGBM training and key insertion) of fast PLBF and fast PLBF++ against the authors' own reimplementation of PLBF, on the Malicious URLs and EMBER datasets, in the memory-budget framework. At N=1000, k=5, fast PLBF is 50.8x (URLs) and 34.3x (EMBER) faster and fast PLBF++ is 63.1x and 39.3x faster; at N=1000, k=50 with a 500 Kb backup-filter budget the figures are 233x/199x and 761x/500x. Fast PLBF gives identical FPR and fast PLBF++ is at most 1.0019x (URLs) and 1.000083x (EMBER) worse; no CPU, Python version or hardware is stated.
status_note: Stale research code: 13 stars, no releases or tags, and only four small commits since 2023 (June 2025: import fix, counting fix, eval scripts, dependency bump). It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor or port, and it is already vendored in the learnedbf PyPI package.
